tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC5341491 (Psychological Medicine 47(5):971-980): Abstract, Discussion, Strengths and limitations and Conclusion read in the adjudicator's own browser tab on 2026-10-31
tasks.extracted: The authors read their results as some evidence that cannabis initiation increases the risk of schizophrenia, with a small causal estimate and any effect of initiation likely to be small, and as strong, stronger, evidence that schizophrenia risk predicts initiation, adding that the weakness of the cannabis instrument limits interpretation. Limitations they state: large overlap between exposure and outcome samples would bias results towards the observational association; the reverse analysis assumes that genetic predictors of schizophrenia act in the general population, most of whom never develop it; MR-Egger tests direct (biological) pleiotropy, not mediated pleiotropy; and a genetic correlation fits shared genetic architecture or causation in either direction.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC7646282 (Lancet Psychiatry 6(5):427-436): text from AI reader 216's saved copy, read by the adjudicator; Figure 1 viewed in the adjudicator's own browser tab on 2026-10-31
tasks.extracted: 901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites, recruited between May 1, 2010, and April 1, 2015. Questions on the type of cannabis made no reference to potency; potency was assigned from THC concentrations by type in a 2016 European report, supplemented by national data. The main text speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency, not of the type mainly used: in Table 2 every person who had used is in one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, potency missing for 3; 251 + 334 = 585 cases; editors' arithmetic). Against never use, fully adjusted (Figure 1): occasional use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (10% or more), use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57, daily use 2.19 and 4.78, the text giving 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6) and 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3); no evidence of interaction between frequency of use and type (p = 0.25). The authors present the daily high-potency finding as a replication of their previous south London study (ref. 28, Di Forti et al., 2015).
